Mainland restaurant brands are expanding rapidly in Hong Kong. Can they turn first-time customers into regulars?

Editor: 查言潞 ZHA YANLUTime: Nov.20, 2026

From Xiao Noodles to CHAGEE, mainland food and drink brands are expanding their store networks in Hong Kong. As they face operating costs and competition, turning first purchases into steady local demand will be key to their long-term prospects.

A coupon from a food delivery app prompted Chen, a 19-year-old student, to try mainland restaurant chain Xiao Noodles for the first time. It didn’t make him a regular.

He ordered tomato-flavoured noodles, but the broth didn’t taste as he had expected. He later tried the chain again in mainland China and still felt the same way.

Asked whether he would go back, Chen said he would only go if he owed the friend who invited him a favour.

“It just tasted awful,” he said.

Meanwhile, Xiao Noodles and CHAGEE have grown to 19 and 23 stores in Hong Kong, respectively. They can draw curious customers when they open, but can these fast-growing mainland brands build a steady local customer base and stay in business for the long term?

Xiao Noodles’ Hong Kong store count

Select a data point to see the count for that date.

Two mainland brands open 42 Hong Kong stores in just over two years

Xiao Noodles entered Hong Kong in May 2024. According to the company’s 2026 interim results, its Hong Kong store count rose from seven a year earlier to 17 by the end of June, an increase of about 143%.

By November 2026, the brand’s official store directory listed 19 Hong Kong stores.

Mainland tea chain CHAGEE entered Hong Kong in September 2024 and had opened seven stores by September 2025. In August 2026, its management said the number had risen to 22. The opening of its Wong Tai Sin Centre store on 29 October brought the total to 23.

CHAGEE’s Hong Kong store count

Select a data point to see the count for that date.

From residential neighbourhoods to major shopping malls, the two chains have expanded into different parts of Hong Kong, giving more consumers a chance to try them.

Other mainland food and drink brands have had a different experience in Hong Kong.

In March 2025, 21st Century Business Herald reported that some mainland brands were continuing to open stores in Hong Kong, while others had ended leases early or closed outlets after struggling to operate. Simon Wong Ka-wo, president of the Hong Kong Federation of Restaurants and Related Trades, told the newspaper that some mainland companies had done too little market research before arriving, assuming a business model that worked on the mainland would carry over directly to Hong Kong.

    The costs and competition behind the expansion

    Rent, wages and ingredients are among the operating costs mainland food and drink brands face when they enter Hong Kong.

    In a December 2025 interview with the Hong Kong Economic Journal, Wong said that rent, labour and ingredients continued to put pressure on Hong Kong’s restaurant trade. Local restaurants were also facing competition from mainland chains with large purchasing operations and established logistics networks.

    For Xiao Noodles, one way to keep its prices competitive is to use the group’s scale to control costs at its Hong Kong restaurants.

    Xiao Noodles vice-president Zhang Haixia told 21st Century Business Herald in March 2025 that having its headquarters nearby in Guangzhou made it easier for the group to manage its Hong Kong operations. The company also brought the digital management systems and self-service ordering it uses on the mainland to its Hong Kong stores.

    She said at the time that 70% of customers placed their own orders by phone, reducing the need for staff to serve diners.

    Xiao Noodles group revenue

    Revenue covers the first half of 2025 and 2026, rounded to the nearest RMB million.

    Xiao Noodles reported group revenue of about RMB939 million for the first half of 2026, up 33.6% from about RMB703 million a year earlier.

    CHAGEE group net revenue

    Net revenue covers the second quarter of 2025 and 2026, rounded to the nearest RMB million.

    CHAGEE has grown its business by expanding its store network. By the second quarter of 2026, the group had 7,639 stores worldwide. Quarterly net revenue reached about RMB3.415 billion, up 2.5% year on year.

    Both companies report these revenue figures for the whole group, so the figures do not show whether their Hong Kong stores are profitable. Local sales, operating costs and how often customers return are important measures of how well the expansion is working.

    From a first purchase to repeat visits

    Billy Mak, an associate professor in Hong Kong Baptist University’s Department of Accountancy, Economics and Finance, told Sing Tao Daily in September 2026 that as spending patterns change, physical stores need to manage costs more efficiently and offer products that are good value or that customers need to experience in person.

    In the same report, Terence Chong, executive director of the Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said younger consumers’ habits were changing. A company’s ability to adapt to what customers want would be especially important to its growth, he said.

    Lin, a university student, has become a regular at Xiao Noodles. He visits about once every two weeks and spends HK$50 to HK$60 on a set meal. He finds the price reasonable and doesn’t wait for a promotion before going.

    In the tea market, promotions are what bring some customers in for the first time.

    Student Zhang first bought CHAGEE in Hong Kong during a buy-one-get-one-free promotion. He had already tried the same brand in Shenzhen. He noticed little difference in taste between the two cities, but the drinks were cheaper in Shenzhen.

    Zhang said he had trouble getting to sleep after drinking CHAGEE and hadn’t bought it since. He would still consider going back if the chain ran another buy-one-get-one-free offer.

    Li, a Hong Kong university student, first chose CHAGEE because there were no other tea shops nearby. He returned because he liked one of its drinks and had bought from the chain about twice in the previous three months.

    He also buys from Ten Ren’s Tea. How far he has to go and how long he will have to queue both factor into his decision.

    Local competition and staying in business

    Wong told 21st Century Business Herald in March 2025 that Hong Kong consumers were becoming more careful about eating out. Compared with high-end restaurants, affordable options such as cha chaan tengs, fast-food outlets and shops selling rice with two dishes had relatively steady customer traffic.

    That gives brands with affordable prices room to grow, while putting them in competition with established local eateries.

    For the same report, a journalist visited Xiao Noodles’ Whampoa store and saw office workers, students and older adults at lunchtime. The brand chose a largely residential neighbourhood for its first Hong Kong store, away from the usual tourist spots and main business districts.

    CHAGEE customers can compare prices and flavours across tea brands before deciding where to buy.

    Li said he would consider making a special trip if CHAGEE introduced a seasonal drink, provided the queue wasn’t too long.

    With 42 stores between them, Xiao Noodles and CHAGEE have built a sizeable presence in Hong Kong. The rise in store numbers alone says little about profitability.

    As they contend with competition and operating costs in Hong Kong’s food and drink market, their ability to keep existing stores performing, manage costs and build a steady local customer base will help determine whether they can sustain their businesses over the long term.
